meaning_en: Counting your chickens before they hatch.
conversation:
Sharmila: Sanyal-babu has already booked a wedding hall for his daughter and that boy from Durgapur.
Paltu: The girl hasn't even met the boy yet! Gachhe kanthal gonphe tel.
correct: Sanyal-babu is preparing for a wedding that hasn't even been agreed.
literal: A man oils his moustache though the jackfruit is still hanging on the tree.
plausible: Sanyal-babu is a careful father who plans everything well in advance.

proverb_bn: ঠাকুর ঘরে কে? আমি কলা খাই না
romanised: Thakur ghore ke? Ami kola khai na.
meaning_en: A guilty person gives themselves away by denying something no one accused them of.
conversation:
Rakhi: Someone deleted the shared sales file this morning.
Bikram: Don't look at me! I never even opened that folder today!
Supriya: Nobody asked you, Bikram. Thakur ghore ke? Ami kola khai na.
correct: Bikram's eager denial, before anyone accused him, suggests he deleted the file.
literal: Someone in the prayer room is saying they don't eat bananas.
plausible: Bikram is clearly innocent, because he says he never opened the folder.

proverb_bn: চোরের দশ দিন, গৃহস্থের এক দিন
romanised: Chorer dosh din, grihosther ek din.
meaning_en: A wrongdoer may get away many times, but is caught in the end.
conversation:
Nilanjan: That shopkeeper cheated customers on his weighing scale for years, and nobody could prove it.
Sumana: And yesterday a food inspector caught him red-handed. Chorer dosh din, grihosther ek din.
correct: The shopkeeper got away with cheating many times but was finally caught.
literal: A thief gets ten days of luck, while the owner of the house gets just one.
plausible: The shopkeeper was unlucky to be caught over one small mistake.

proverb_bn: পড়েছি মোগলের হাতে, খানা খেতে হবে সাথে
romanised: Porechhi Mogoler hate, khana khete hobe sathe.
meaning_en: When you are in someone's power, you have to go along with them.
conversation:
Sourav: You're up at five doing yoga? You never open your eyes before nine.
Bappa: The new hostel warden has made it compulsory, and he can throw us out. Porechhi Mogoler hate, khana khete hobe sathe.
correct: Bappa does the yoga only because the warden has power over him.
literal: A prisoner of the Mughals must sit down and eat every meal with them.
plausible: Bappa has decided on his own to become an early riser.

proverb_bn: পাগলে কী না বলে, ছাগলে কী না খায়
romanised: Pagole ki na bole, chhagole ki na khay.
meaning_en: Don't take the nonsense of foolish people seriously.
conversation:
Anjali: Boro-pishi told everyone at the wedding that our new bou is unlucky because it rained.
Ritwik: Boro-pishi says something like that at every wedding. Pagole ki na bole, chhagole ki na khay.
correct: Ritwik thinks Boro-pishi's remark is silly talk that nobody should take to heart.
literal: There is nothing at all that a madman won't say, and nothing that a goat won't chew.
plausible: Ritwik agrees that the rain on the wedding day really was a bad sign.

proverb_bn: পাগলে কী না বলে, ছাগলে কী না খায়
romanised: Pagole ki na bole, chhagole ki na khay.
meaning_en: Don't take the nonsense of foolish people seriously.
conversation:
Rafiq: The man in the next flat is telling the whole building that I'm a spy because I work at night.
Nadia: He also says his cat talks to him. Pagole ki na bole, chhagole ki na khay.
correct: Nadia tells Rafiq not to worry about the neighbour's absurd accusation.
literal: Crazy people say anything at all, just as goats eat anything.
plausible: Nadia thinks Rafiq should stop working at night so as to avoid suspicion.

meaning_en: When a duty is shared by many, nobody does it.
conversation:
Nupur: The building's water pump has been broken for two weeks. Hasn't anyone called a plumber?
Bubai: All twelve flats think someone else will do it. Bhager ma Ganga pay na.
correct: Because the job belongs to everyone, no single resident has taken care of it.
literal: A mother with many sons never gets taken to the river Ganga.
plausible: The plumber himself has flatly refused to come to their building.

meaning_en: When a duty is shared by many, nobody does it.
conversation:
Joy: Why hasn't the group report been submitted? The deadline was yesterday.
Srabanti: Five of us were supposed to write the conclusion, and each one thought another had already done it. Bhager ma Ganga pay na.
correct: Since the task was shared, nobody in the group actually did it.
literal: A mother divided among her children never reaches the Ganga.
plausible: The report was late because the conclusion was too difficult to write.

meaning_en: Fake sympathy from someone who doesn't really care.
conversation:
Pinki: Chhoto-kaka was crying at Jethu's shraddha, but they hadn't spoken for ten years because of the property.
Dida: Machher mayer putroshok. He was the first to ask about the will.
correct: Chhoto-kaka's tears at the ceremony were insincere.
literal: A fish's mother weeps bitterly over a dead son.
plausible: Chhoto-kaka felt deep regret for the years they didn't speak.

meaning_en: A quarrel or problem always involves both sides.
conversation:
Soma: Mrs Dutta says the Boses started the fight over the parking spot.
Pradip: And the Boses say the Duttas started it. Ek hate tali baje na.
correct: Pradip thinks both families share the blame for the fight.
literal: You can't make a clapping sound with just one hand on its own.
plausible: Pradip believes the Boses alone are to blame for it.

meaning_en: A quarrel or problem always involves both sides.
conversation:
Mitu: Ma, Arko never listens. Every argument we have is his fault.
Ma: And you hang up on him every single time. Ek hate tali baje na.
correct: Ma thinks Mitu also plays a part in the arguments.
literal: One palm on its own cannot produce the sound of a clap.
plausible: Ma agrees that Arko is entirely at fault here.

proverb_bn: দাঁত থাকতে দাঁতের মর্যাদা বোঝে না
romanised: Dant thakte danter morjada bojhe na.
meaning_en: We don't value what we have until we lose it.
conversation:
Arif: I left my old job because the manager was strict, but at least he trained us properly. My new boss doesn't care at all.
Moushumi: Dant thakte danter morjada bojhe na.
correct: Arif didn't appreciate his old manager until he no longer had him.
literal: Teeth are not valued while they are still there in the mouth.
plausible: Moushumi thinks Arif's new boss will turn out to be better in the end.

meaning_en: Looking for trouble when everything is going fine.
conversation:
Shubhra: You had a secure government job with good hours. Why on earth did you quit to sell pickles online?
Neel: I don't know, I was bored. Shukhe thakte bhute kiloy, I suppose.
correct: Neel admits he went looking for trouble when his life was comfortable.
literal: A ghost comes and hits a person who is living happily.
plausible: Neel quit because the government job paid him far too badly.

meaning_en: Looking for trouble when everything is going fine.
conversation:
Lubna: Kamal had a happy marriage, and he started secretly chatting with his ex. Now his wife has found out.
Sharif: Shukhe thakte bhute kiloy.
correct: Kamal spoiled a good situation by going looking for trouble.
literal: A ghost comes along and thumps someone who is at ease.
plausible: Sharif thinks Kamal's marriage was already unhappy long before this.

proverb_bn: যার বিয়ে তার হুঁশ নেই, পাড়াপড়শির ঘুম নেই
romanised: Jar biye tar hunsh nei, parapoershir ghum nei.
meaning_en: Outsiders fuss more than the person actually concerned.
conversation:
Sudipta: Tomorrow is Rahul's board exam, and he's playing PUBG. His aunts have called me ten times today.
Bonny: Jar biye tar hunsh nei, parapoershir ghum nei.
correct: Everyone around Rahul is far more anxious about the exam than he is.
literal: The groom doesn't care, but the neighbours can't get any sleep.
plausible: Bonny thinks Rahul's aunts should stop calling about the exam.

proverb_bn: যার বিয়ে তার হুঁশ নেই, পাড়াপড়শির ঘুম নেই
romanised: Jar biye tar hunsh nei, parapoershir ghum nei.
meaning_en: Outsiders fuss more than the person actually concerned.
conversation:
Riya: It's Ashok-da's flat being renovated, but it's the other residents who argue about the tiles every evening.
Zahid: Jar biye tar hunsh nei, parapoershir ghum nei.
correct: Outsiders are fussing over the flat more than its owner is.
literal: The groom is unbothered, but the neighbours have lost sleep.
plausible: Zahid thinks Ashok-da should let the residents choose the tiles for him.

proverb_bn: রাজায় রাজায় যুদ্ধ হয়, উলুখাগড়ার প্রাণ যায়
romanised: Rajay rajay juddho hoy, ulukhagrar pran jay.
meaning_en: When the powerful fight, ordinary people suffer.
conversation:
Tareq: The two big parties called rival hartals, and my rickshaw-puller neighbour hasn't earned a taka all week.
Shahana: Rajay rajay juddho hoy, ulukhagrar pran jay.
correct: The parties' fight is hurting ordinary people like the rickshaw-puller.
literal: Whenever kings fight one another, the humble reeds growing nearby get killed.
plausible: Shahana thinks the rickshaw-puller should join one of the parties.

meaning_en: People will pay any price for something they love.
conversation:
Indranil: Baba paid fifteen thousand for a vintage fountain pen he'll never actually write with.
Keya: Shokher tola ashi taka.
correct: People will pay any price for something they love.
literal: The hobby cost Baba eighty rupees for every tola.
plausible: Keya thinks Baba was cheated and paid far too much for the pen.

proverb_bn: কানে দিয়েছি তুলো, পিঠে বেঁধেছি কুলো
romanised: Kane diyechhi tulo, pithe bendhechhi kulo.
meaning_en: Being completely shameless and immune to criticism.
conversation:
Swarup: The whole para complains about the loudspeakers at your club's puja, and you've made them even louder?
Bablu: Kane diyechhi tulo, pithe bendhechhi kulo.
correct: Bablu is completely unbothered by everyone's criticism of him.
literal: Bablu has stuffed cotton in his ears and tied a winnowing fan to his back.
plausible: Bablu is sorry and will turn the loudspeakers down soon.

meaning_en: Everyone is guilty; if you remove the dishonest, no one is left.
conversation:
Pritam: The new principal wants to sack every teacher who gives private tuition.
Jhuma: Thog bachhte ga ujar.
correct: Almost every teacher does it, so hardly anyone would be left.
literal: If you pick out all the cheats in the village, the whole village will be empty.
plausible: Jhuma thinks only one or two of the teachers give private tuition.

meaning_en: Two people or things that are too different can't get along.
conversation:
Abir: Why did they make Ronit and Sayak share a project? One plans everything, the other does everything at the last minute.
Mitali: Tele jole mish khay na.
correct: Ronit and Sayak are too different to work well together.
literal: Oil poured into water will never blend into it at all.
plausible: Mitali thinks Ronit and Sayak will make a perfect team on the project.

meaning_en: Two people or things that are too different can't get along.
conversation:
Debosmita: My father is a die-hard Mohun Bagan fan and my father-in-law is East Bengal to the bone. Every family dinner ends in a fight.
Farhan: Tele jole mish khay na.
correct: The two fathers are far too different ever to get along.
literal: Oil and water simply cannot mix, however long you stir them together.
plausible: Farhan thinks the two fathers secretly enjoy their dinner fights.

meaning_en: Trying to force a dull person to become brilliant.
conversation:
Swarnali: Mrs Sen has hired four tutors to make her son crack IIT, and he can't even do class-eight maths.
Hirak: Gadha pitiye ghora kora.
correct: She is trying to force a weak student to become brilliant.
literal: Mrs Sen is beating a donkey hard in the hope of turning it into a horse.
plausible: Hirak thinks four tutors will surely get the boy into IIT.

meaning_en: Trying to force a dull person to become brilliant.
conversation:
Monir: The club's owner keeps paying coaches to turn his nephew into a striker, but the boy can't even kick straight.
Nazneen: Gadha pitiye ghora kora.
correct: The owner is trying to force a talentless boy into a star.
literal: The owner keeps beating a donkey to make it into a horse.
plausible: Nazneen thinks the nephew is just one good coach away from greatness.

meaning_en: Trying to force a dull person to become brilliant.
conversation:
Anurag: The company sent the new hire to five leadership trainings, but he still can't run a ten-minute meeting.
Samiha: Gadha pitiye ghora kora.
correct: The company is trying to force an unsuitable person into a leader.
literal: They are beating a donkey in the hope it turns into a horse.
plausible: Samiha thinks one more training will make him a great leader.

meaning_en: An old person behaving in a youthful, unsuitable way.
conversation:
Shahjahan: My sixty-five-year-old uncle has started posting TikTok dance videos in a baseball cap.
Laila: Buro shaliker ghare ron.
correct: The uncle is acting youthful in a way that doesn't suit his age.
literal: Fresh feathers have sprouted on an old myna's neck.
plausible: Laila thinks the uncle is earning good money from TikTok.

meaning_en: Good deeds should be done without delay.
conversation:
Anindita: I want to apologise to Mitul for what I said at the party, but I'll wait for a good moment.
Shafin: Shubhoshyo shighrom.
correct: The right thing should be done at once, without waiting for a moment.
literal: The auspicious moment Anindita wants will come very quickly.
plausible: Shafin thinks Anindita should wait for the right moment before apologising.

proverb_bn: সুঁই হয়ে ঢোকে, ফাল হয়ে বেরোয়
romanised: Shui hoye dhoke, phal hoye beroy.
meaning_en: Someone who starts small and humble, then takes over.
conversation:
Joyanta: The new app only wanted my phone number at first. Now it reads my contacts, location and messages.
Laboni: Shui hoye dhoke, phal hoye beroy.
correct: The app asked for very little at first and has gradually taken over.
literal: It goes in as a needle and comes back out as a ploughshare.
plausible: Laboni thinks the app needs all that data to work properly.

meaning_en: If you are good to others, others are good to you.
conversation:
Ashraf: My new boss was strict with everyone, but after I helped her with the move, she's been kind to me every day.
Tahera: Apni bhalo to jogot bhalo.
correct: Ashraf was kind to his boss, so she has been kind to him in return.
literal: If you are fine yourself, then the whole world is also fine.
plausible: Tahera thinks the boss is only being kind to get a favour.

meaning_en: Wrongdoing always catches up with the wrongdoer.
conversation:
Abdur: The officer who took bribes for thirty years was finally caught on his last day before retirement.
Momena: Pap bapkeo chhare na.
correct: The officer's wrongdoing caught up with him in the end.
literal: Sin does not spare anyone, not even the officer's own father.
plausible: Momena thinks the officer was caught only because of office jealousy.

proverb_bn: সাধে কি বাবা বলি, গুঁতোর চোটে বাবা বলি
romanised: Shadhe ki baba boli, gunttor chote baba boli.
meaning_en: Showing respect only because one is forced to.
conversation:
Kibria: Why do you keep praising the union leader on Facebook? You hate him.
Rajon: He decides who gets the overtime. Shadhe ki baba boli, gunttor chote baba boli.
correct: Rajon praises the leader only because he is forced to.
literal: He calls him father not out of love but because of the jabs.
plausible: Rajon has truly come to like the union leader after all this time.

proverb_bn: সাধে কি বাবা বলি, গুঁতোর চোটে বাবা বলি
romanised: Shadhe ki baba boli, gunttor chote baba boli.
meaning_en: Showing respect only because one is forced to.
conversation:
Moyukh: The new director makes us all clap after his boring speeches, and you clap the loudest.
Faria: My appraisal is next month. Shadhe ki baba boli, gunttor chote baba boli.
correct: Faria shows the director respect only because she is under pressure.
literal: She calls him father only because of the jabs, not from love.
plausible: Faria truly enjoys the director's speeches more than anyone.

meaning_en: When in Rome, do as the Romans do.
conversation:
Pragya: At the Bihu festival in Assam, our Kolkata group learned the dance steps and wore gamosas like everyone else.
Riyad: Joshmin deshe jodachar.
correct: The group followed the local customs of the place they visited.
literal: Every land in the world has its own particular set of customs and ways.
plausible: Riyad thinks the group was only joking around at the festival.

proverb_bn: সব পাখি মাছ খায়, দোষ হয় মাছরাঙার
romanised: Shob pakhi machh khay, dosh hoy machhrangar.
meaning_en: One person is blamed for what everyone does.
conversation:
Shafiul: All the shops on our street sell without receipts, but the tax officer fined only the old tailor.
Akhi: Shob pakhi machh khay, dosh hoy machhrangar.
correct: Only the tailor is being punished for what every shop does.
literal: Every bird eats fish, yet the kingfisher is the only one that gets blamed.
plausible: Akhi thinks the tailor cheated on his taxes far more than others.

meaning_en: Using what you learned from someone against them.
conversation:
Swarnava: I taught my nephew chess, and now he beats me every Sunday with the very openings I showed him.
Rumaisa: Guru mara bidya.
correct: The nephew is beating him with the very moves he taught.
literal: The nephew has learned a skill for killing his teacher.
plausible: Rumaisa thinks Swarnava lets his nephew win on purpose every Sunday.
